The insect was surprisingly heavy. Taking everything into account, I could hardly blame Jupiter for what he thought about it. But why Legrand agreed with him was beyond me.

‘I sent for you,’ he said grandly after I finished examining the beetle, ‘because I wanted your advice and help in carrying out the intentions of Fate and this bug—’

‘My dear Legrand,’ I interrupted, ‘you are clearly unwell and ought to take care of yourself. You must go to bed. I'll stay with you for a few days until you recover. You have a fever and—’

‘Take my pulse,’ he said.

I did, and I must admit that I found no sign of fever at all.

‘Still, you can be ill without a fever. Just this once, let me decide what's best for you. First, go to bed. Then—’

‘You're wrong,’ he broke in. ‘I'm as well as anyone could expect, considering how excited I am. If you truly want to help me, help calm that excitement.’

‘And how can I do that?’

‘Easily enough. Jupiter and I are planning a trip into the hills on the mainland. We need someone we can rely on to help us, and you are the only person we trust. Whether we succeed or fail, the agitation you see in me now will settle down.’

‘I want to help in any way I can,’ I answered. ‘But are you saying that this wretched beetle has something to do with your expedition into the hills?’

‘It does.’

‘Then, Legrand, I refuse to take part in anything so ridiculous.’

‘I'm sorry—very sorry. We'll have to attempt it alone.’

‘Alone! The man must be mad! But wait—how long do you intend to be away?’

‘Probably the entire night. We'll leave at once, and whatever happens, we'll return by sunrise.’

‘Will you give me your word of honour that, once this strange adventure is over and the business with the bug—good God!—is settled to your satisfaction, you'll come home and follow my advice exactly, as though I were your doctor?’

‘Yes, I promise. Now let's go; we have no time to waste.’

With a heavy heart, I went along with my friend. We set off at about four o'clock: Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and I. Jupiter carried the scythe and the spades, insisting on taking every one of them himself. This seemed less a sign of eagerness to work or to please than of fear that either kind of tool might fall within his master's reach.

Then the ringmaster made a short speech. He hoped there would be no disturbance, he said. If the man promised to cause no more trouble, he could ride, provided he thought he could stay on the horse. Everyone laughed and agreed, and the man climbed on. The moment he did, the horse began bucking, leaping, and plunging about. Two circus men clung to the bridle, trying to restrain it, while the drunk hugged its neck and his heels flew up with every jump. The whole crowd stood, shouting and laughing until tears ran down their faces. At last, despite everything the circus men did, the horse broke free. Off it tore around the ring, with the drunk lying along its back and clutching its neck. First one leg dangled nearly to the ground on one side, then the other leg on the other side. The audience went wild. I didn't find it funny, though. Seeing the danger he was in made me shake all over. Soon he struggled into a sitting position, straddled the horse, and caught the bridle, swaying from side to side. The next minute he sprang up, let go of the bridle, and stood on the horse's back! And the horse was still racing along at full speed. He stood there riding around as comfortably as if he'd never been drunk in his life. Then he started stripping off his clothes and throwing them away. So many flew off that they almost filled the air. Altogether he removed seventeen outfits. There he stood at last, slim and handsome, wearing the brightest, finest costume you ever saw. He urged the horse on with his whip and made it fly around the ring. Finally he jumped down, bowed, and danced off to the dressing room while everyone roared with delight and amazement.

Then the ringmaster realized he'd been fooled. I reckon you never saw a more miserable-looking ringmaster. Why, the fellow was one of his own performers! He had thought up the whole joke himself and hadn't told a soul. I felt pretty foolish about being taken in, but I wouldn't have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. Maybe there are better circuses somewhere; I don't know. I haven't found one yet. This one was certainly good enough for me, and whenever I come across it again, it can count on getting my business.

He wrote that he was wasting his days to no purpose where he remained, and that the friends he had made in London had sent letters urging his return to conclude their negotiations concerning his venture in India. He could postpone his departure no further. Since his journey to London might be followed by his longer voyage even sooner than he presently supposed, he implored me to give him as much of my company as I could. He therefore begged me to abandon my lonely island and join him at Perth, so that we might travel south together. His letter restored me in some measure to life, and I resolved to leave the island in two days' time.

Before leaving, however, I had a duty to fulfil, the mere thought of which made me shudder. My chemical instruments had to be packed, and to do so I must return to the room of my abominable labours and touch the implements whose very appearance sickened me. At dawn the following morning, I gathered enough courage to unlock the laboratory door. Across the floor lay the remnants of the unfinished creature I had destroyed. I felt almost as though I had torn apart the living body of a human being. After pausing to regain control of myself, I stepped inside. My hand shook as I carried the instruments out. It occurred to me, however, that the remains of my work must not be left behind to arouse the villagers' fear and suspicion. I placed them in a basket with a considerable weight of stones and set it aside, intending to cast it into the sea that same night. Meanwhile, I seated myself on the shore and occupied myself with cleaning and putting my chemical equipment in order.

The change in my feelings since the dæmon's appearance that night could not have been more absolute. Previously I had contemplated my promise in dark despair, as an obligation that must be honoured whatever its results. Now it seemed that a veil had been lifted from my sight, and I could see distinctly for the first time. Not for a single instant did I consider returning to my task. His threat burdened my mind, but I did not think of any willing action of my own as a means of escaping it. I had decided that making a second being like the fiend I had already created would constitute selfishness of the vilest and most dreadful kind. Every thought that might have led me to another judgment I drove from my mind.
